title: keyboard.spec.ts:275 asserts the ? sheet's <kbd> count and never a chord, so no browser assertion distinguishes the effective chord from the default
detail: FOUND BY PLAN 5 TASK 5 (commit 4698f233), while proving every locator this plan re-pointed red. keyboard.spec.ts:275 is `await expect(sheet.locator("kbd")).toHaveCount(20)` — a COUNT, and the count is a property of the projection's membership (`productShortcutIds()` reads PRODUCT_SHORTCUTS either way), not of the chord each row prints. MEASURED, not reasoned: with `activeShortcuts()` in shortcut-manager/bindings.ts forced to return PRODUCT_SHORTCUTS, `npx playwright test keyboard.spec.ts` is 4 passed — the sheet still renders twenty rows and the file never rebinds, so nothing in it measures effective-vs-default. The behaviour IS guarded, but only in jsdom, and by two files: settings-keyboard.dom.test.tsx:190 and shortcut-reference.dom.test.tsx:70-91 both redden on the same break (`expected 'Ctrl+Shift+P' to be 'Ctrl+J'`). So a rebind that reached the Keyboard tab but stopped reaching the `?` sheet would ship. NOT FIXED HERE: it is not a broken locator but missing coverage, the fix is a rebinding step in a suite this plan does not own, and plan 6 (iconography-and-copy) owns the accessible-name/copy census this file sits in. The fix is one step in keyboard.spec.ts: rebind a chord through the tab, then assert the sheet prints the rebound chord rather than the default. TASK 2.4b, 2026-10-12: CLOSED fixed. The cell's run (npx playwright test keyboard.spec.ts --grep sheet --workers=1) collects two real cases, both passed on desktop-chromium and skipped on phone, and it reproduces the row's own count: sheet.locator('kbd').toHaveCount(20) is satisfied at this sha, as a projection membership and never as a chord — which is the row's complaint and why the 20 being right closes nothing. What closes it is the case the row prescribed, added to keyboard.spec.ts: a rebind of publish.surface to Ctrl+J through the Keyboard tab's own arm control, then the ? sheet's own row asserted to print the rebound chord. Red-proofed the way this row measured its own defect: with activeShortcuts() forced to return PRODUCT_SHORTCUTS the whole file is 5 passed / 6 skipped and that case is the single failure, which is what nothing in the file did before it.
check: keyboard.spec.ts rebinds publish.surface to Ctrl+J through the Keyboard tab's own arm control and asserts the ? sheet's own row prints the rebound chord rather than the default, so a browser assertion now distinguishes the effective chord from the default; the sheet's kbd count stays 20 as the projection's membership, which is why the count never was that assertion. Red-proofed: with activeShortcuts() forced to return PRODUCT_SHORTCUTS the whole file is 5 passed, 6 skipped, and this case is the one failure.

title: The inspector's field funnel refuses an unparseable value on every geometry branch except the Line endpoints, which write Number(value) unchecked
detail: FOUND BY Task 9 candidate rank 6 (2026-10-12), while establishing whether a Line's scalar writes had a destination owner; it reported the asymmetry and did not establish its cause, which is why it is a row and not a fix. `selection-inspector/panel.ts:650` writes `object.set(key, Number(value))` for the `shape-line-` fields with no finiteness check, while the branch directly above it validates and refuses -- `const parsed = parsedPath(String(value)); if (parsed === undefined) return false;`. A non-numeric field value would therefore reach `object.set` as `NaN` on the Line branch and be refused on the branch above it. VERIFIED by the controller: both branches read as described. NOT ESTABLISHED: reachability -- the inspector may refuse a non-finite edit upstream of this funnel, so the unchecked write may be dead rather than live. What settles it is one inspector field driven with a non-numeric string, which is a browser check; the phase that found it forbids behaviour changes, so nothing was altered. TASK 2.4b, 2026-10-12: FIXED, and the browser half is NOT verified. writeShapeGeometryField's Line branch now refuses a non-finite endpoint through the same finiteness the branch above uses, and the guard is red-proofed: removing it reddens the new case at panel.dom.test.ts ('expected true to be false'). Reachability is measured in jsdom rather than in a browser: ControlNumber's own parse refuses a non-numeric draft before it commits, so no field reaches the funnel with one, which is why the guard belongs to the funnel and not only to the control. The browser drive is NOT verified: a probe on the built preview could not type into [data-vigilia-shape-line=x1] at all — a Playwright fill never settled and a keyboard drive left the field at its starting value — so the funnel was exercised by no browser here, and the field-level refusal is asserted in panel.dom.test.ts instead. The cell's own command was run for collection alone, with no browser and no port: npx playwright test tests/e2e/inspector-sections.spec.ts --grep gives every kind a column --list exits 0 with two entries, one case at inspector-sections.spec.ts:574 -- gives every kind a column, and shows no kind a property it lacks -- under both desktop-chromium and phone-chromium, so the cell collects a real case and drives the kind-aware branch the Line endpoints funnel sits behind; what it does not do is exercise a non-finite endpoint through the field.
check: the Line endpoints branch of the inspector's field funnel refuses a non-finite value before it writes one: writeShapeGeometryField against a Line returns false with both endpoints unchanged, and removing the Number.isFinite guard reddens panel.dom.test.ts (expected true to be false), while reachability is established in jsdom alone: ControlNumber's own parse refused a non-numeric draft there, which is the closest this row got to an answer and is not a browser result, so no claim is made here that a non-numeric draft reaches the funnel in the product.

One ruling covers all three; Task 4.1 of the backlog-drain plan is where it is applied.

title: The ceiling over editor-shell.css counts violations, so a swap - one violation corrected while another arrives - leaves it green and the file's residual set unread
detail: FOUND BY PLAN 8 TASK 9 (2026-10-11), while landing the ceiling it names. `scripts/design-tokens.mjs`'s `CEILINGS` caps `src/web/packages/editor/src/editor-shell/editor-shell.css` at 58 violations, and it is green at HEAD. It compares a *count*, so it cannot see WHICH violations they are: fix one of the 24 spacing values and let a different literal arrive in the same commit and the count is unchanged at 58 - green - while the set the exemptions were measured against has moved. Three of the 61 are keyed on their own text (`margin-right: 62px`, `92px`, `122px`) and so cannot be swapped silently; the other 55 can. CONSEQUENCE: the instrument reads as capping the file's residuals while it caps only their number, so a surface can drift in one place and be repaired in another with no failure anywhere. WHAT WOULD CLOSE IT: read the violation SET rather than its size - a per-key allowlist of rule plus value (the shape the three exemptions already use, extended to the whole file) or a comparison against the recorded list - each a different instrument from the one this task was scoped to build. NOT FIXED HERE: the plan mandates the count shape (Task 9 Step 1, a row that fails above the measured count and passes at or below it), and widening it decides what the file's residuals are *allowed to be*, which is a design decision rather than a task. SECOND INSTANCE, ONE RUNG FURTHER - PLAN 8'S FINAL WHOLE-BRANCH REVIEW (2026-10-11): an exemption is not a site either. `scripts/design-tokens.mjs:283-289` filters the exemptions on `violation.text`, so a second `margin-right: 62px` added anywhere in the file would be exempt too - the count would not rise and the dead-exemption guard would not fire, because the keyed text still exists once. The finding above says a count is not a set; this says a key is not a line. NOT FIXED: the exemption shape is Task 9's mandated one, and keying on site as well as text is a different instrument. IT IS NOT `vg-274`, which is the file's exposure to the ratchet at all; this is the coverage of the instrument built to cap it. Same family as `vg-271`/`vg-274`/`vg-286`/`vg-292`: an acceptance instrument claiming more coverage than it has - and here the count IS the deliberately chosen shape, so the finding is the limit of the fix rather than a defect in it.
check: `CEILINGS[0]` in `scripts/design-tokens.mjs` is `max: 0` over editor-shell.css's whole recorded residual set and each violation carries the `site` it sits at, so a swap fails as `counted` and a departure as `dead`, and an exemption is keyed on the site as well as the text; `design:check` exits 0 and the self-test fails when the set is replaced by its count

title: designLanguagePx carries 1.6, 1.7 and 1.8 as stroke widths but the scanner regex needs a px suffix, so those three entries can never fire and the plan states they guard stroke widths
detail: FOUND WHILE APPLYING THE WEIGHT RULING (2026-10-11) in plan 6 Task 2b, by asking the brief's question empirically instead of assuming the answer. The task was to decide whether the new 10px tier weight of 2 had to be added to `scripts/design-tokens.gated.json`'s `designLanguagePx`. It does not, and the cause is not about 2: `scripts/design-tokens.mjs` matches px with the regex `(d+(?:.d+)?)px`, which requires the literal suffix. A bare numeric literal is invisible to it, so the three stroke-width entries already in `designLanguagePx` -- 1.6, 1.7 and 1.8, alongside 3, 11, 14, 26, 30, 32, 36, 46, 74, 246, 276 and 999 -- have never gated anything. The proof is in the tree rather than in a reading: `icons.ts` is a gated file and it held `GLYPH_STROKE_WIDTH = 1.75` for two commits, a value absent from `designLanguagePx`, with `design:check` exiting 0 throughout. WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND A DEAD ENTRY, and this is the part that is a defect rather than a tidy-up: plan 6 Global Constraints states the opposite belief in words -- "section 6's 1.6-1.8 are already in designLanguagePx, so a stroke width is legitimate where a spacing value would not be" -- so a future reader is told the allowlist is what licenses a stroke width, when the allowlist cannot see one and the DOM assertion is the only thing that ever has. That sentence is now the misleading half and needs correcting wherever the weight ruling propagated, which Task 2b did not do because the brief scoped propagation to the rule itself. NOT FIXED ON THE FLY: removing the three dead entries and correcting the sentence are both small, but they are a decision about whether designLanguagePx should keep values that only a px-suffixed CSS stroke could use -- `editor-shell.css` may legitimately write `stroke-width: 1.7px` -- and that is a read of the CSS before anyone deletes anything. WHAT WOULD CLOSE IT: either the three entries are shown to be reachable from a px-suffixed site and kept with a comment saying which, or they are removed, and Global Constraints says plainly that the text scan does not gate stroke widths and the DOM case does. RELATED: `vg-192` is the same family of claim -- a gate believed to cover something it cannot see.
check: the 1.6, 1.7 and 1.8 stroke entries are gone from `designLanguagePx`, and `unconsumedPx` in `scripts/design-tokens.mjs` reports and drops any entry no file the run reads writes in `px` form — a bare-number `strokeWidth` is the shape its self-test names

title: The sweep's dispatch gate lists omit steps CI runs, so two tasks reported green over a build that was red on `format:check`
detail: FOUND BY Task 6's lane (2026-10-12) and reported as a concern rather than fixed, correctly, because the offending files sit in `packages/**` and outside that task's scope. MEASURED: `npm run format:check` exited 1 with `Found 3 errors` at HEAD `b9e96c2d`, and `.github/workflows/ci.yml:38` runs it -- FIRST, before `lint` at `:41`, so the build would have failed immediately. The three files were `packages/scene-fabric/src/background-media.ts` (Task 5's `47658230`) and `packages/editor/src/snap-manager/scaling/{rectangular-scale-interaction,scale-snapping-runtime}.ts` (Task 4's `93bb2c5f`). CAUSE ESTABLISHED: removing an `export` keyword shortened each alias's collapsed form below biome's 80-column width, so `biome format` now folds it onto one line -- `export type ScaleRuntimeStep = PlannedScaleRuntimeStep | DuplicateScaleRuntimeStep;` is 85 columns and its keyword-less form 78. THE FORMATTING ITSELF WAS FIXED ON THE FLY at `c65cc0d6`, and `format:check` is green after it. THIS ROW IS ABOUT WHAT LET IT THROUGH, which the fix does not close. Neither Task 4's nor Task 5's dispatch named `format:check`; both lanes ran `npm run lint` and reported the gates green, and `lint` is `biome lint ..`, which does not run the formatter, so the two are genuinely different commands and 'lint is green' was true and insufficient. READING `ci.yml` IN FULL widens the finding beyond that one step: the dispatches named typecheck, lint and the touched tests, while CI also runs `status:check` (`:44`), `hooks:check` (`:50`), `npx vitest run` (`:62`), three vite builds -- player (`:65`), editor (`:72`), host (`:88`) -- `build:fixture` (`:82`), `check-size.mjs` against the player bundle (`:92`) and `playwright test` (`:104`). Task 6's lane covered several of those by its own judgment and that is the only reason this was caught. WHY IT OUTLIVES THE PLAN: a dispatch's gate list is what the next plan's briefs copy, so the omission reproduces wherever a brief restates CI from memory. FIX DIRECTION: have the dispatch name `.github/workflows/ci.yml` as the authority for what 'green' means rather than restating its steps -- a list is exactly the artifact that rots, which is the same failure `vg-347`'s correction and this plan's stale counts both are. title: The licences CI job fails on four packages declared in a manifest but absent from `THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md`, and nothing sees it because CI never runs on `develop`
detail: FOUND BY Task 6's independent review of the dead-code sweep (2026-10-12), while establishing whether the CI steps this sweep's dispatches never named were green at HEAD; REPRODUCED by the controller with the job's own logic before this row was written. MEASURED at HEAD: replicating `.github/workflows/ci.yml`'s `licences` job -- the step that derives every non-`@vigilia/` name from all `src/web/**/package.json` and exits 1 unless `grep -qiF` finds each one in `THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md` -- yields 27 declared names and 4 missing: `@playwright/mcp`, `class-variance-authority`, `clsx`, `tailwind-merge`. The job exits 1. The step is worth reading before touching it: an earlier version of this same job reported green from the day it was written until 2026-09-15 because a failed derivation left its name list empty and the loop unentered, and the comment above it now says a guard that cannot fail is worse than no guard. ALREADY RED AT THE SWEEP'S LANE BASE `86398b1f`, so it is not this sweep's damage; the reviewer attributes the onset to `d26dc7c5`. WHY IT WENT UNNOTICED, which is the part worth keeping: `.github/workflows/ci.yml` never runs on `develop`, the branch this work lands on, so that branch has no CI signal at all -- the same blindness the sweep's own gate-list omission produced (`vg-384`), arriving from a different cause. FIX DIRECTION ESTABLISHED BUT DELIBERATELY NOT TAKEN: `AGENTS.md` requires a shipped dependency's licence to be verified from package metadata and both `THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md` and `docs/engineering/dependencies.md` updated, so the repair is four VERIFIED entries rather than four lines, and asserting a licence is a claim about third-party terms -- which is why this is a row and not a fix on the fly. NOT ESTABLISHED: which of the four are shipped rather than development-only (`@playwright/mcp` is plausibly tooling), and whether `docs/engineering/dependencies.md` is in the same state. The job does not distinguish `dependencies` from `devDependencies`, so the notices' own convention decides that.
check: the four licence names are in `THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md` — class-variance-authority, clsx, tailwind-merge and @playwright/mcp — and `.github/workflows/ci.yml` triggers on `develop` as well as `main`, so the `licences` job sees this branch

title: No command runs the rebuild or display Playwright suites, because playwright.config.ts testIgnores them and nothing passes --config, so their reds are invisible to every gate
detail:
SPLIT OUT OF vg-119 BY PLAN 5 TASK 4A PART I'S CLOSE (2026-10-10), because vg-119's title carries two independent claims and only one of them was fixed. vg-119's first half - the display proof suite red on a run colour the document does not carry - is verified fixed (see that row's addendum). Its second half, "and no command runs that suite", is this row, and it is the reason the first half stayed red long enough to be filed at all. MEASURED BY THE CONTROLLER at head 846e451c: `src/web/playwright.config.ts:114-124` puts both projects' `testIgnore` over `REBUILD_SPEC`, `DISPLAY_SPEC`, `HOST_SPECS` and `PUBLISH_SPEC`; `playwright.rebuild.config.ts:20` and `playwright.display.config.ts:21` are the only runners those two specs have, and each matches exactly one of them; **`grep -n -- '--config' src/web/package.json` returns nothing, and `grep -rn -- '--config' .github/workflows/` returns nothing** - `.github/workflows/ci.yml:104` runs bare `npx playwright test`, and `visual-evidence.yml:49` runs `npx playwright test --project=… --grep=…`, both against the default config. So the two suites run only when a human or an agent types `--config` by hand. CONSEQUENCE, and it is not hypothetical: the harness reds that plans 3, 4 and 5 each discovered separately - vg-119's colour, vg-253's 16 selectOption sites, and the `sectionIds` scoping plan 5 Task 4a part i fixed on the fly - were all reachable by a plain `npx playwright test --config playwright.display.config.ts` and by nothing else, so every gate reported green while three suites were red. `inspector-sections.spec.ts` is in the DEFAULT config, which is why the same round's re-point break was reachable - and was still missed, because the round ran targeted greps rather than the suite. NOT FIXED HERE because the fix is a decision about the gate rather than about the specs: adding a script changes what every future session pays for a full run, and the display suite alone took 11.4 minutes when vg-119 was measured. OWNER: whoever owns the browser-gate scripts (`src/web/package.json` and `.github/workflows/`). Related: vg-192 (tests/e2e belongs to no tsconfig, so a type error there is caught by neither typecheck nor Playwright) - the same class of invisible-to-every-gate defect.

RULED 2026-10-12: RULED 2026-10-12 by the user: WIRE BOTH SUITES, BUT NOT ON EVERY PUSH. The rebuild and display Playwright suites gain a script and a CI job that runs them on workflow_dispatch and on a nightly schedule rather than on every push -- the display suite alone measured 11.4 minutes, and per-push is the cost this ruling refuses while being invisible to every gate is the defect it fixes. The hand-run instruction stays for a session that needs one suite now, so a red is visible on the job that was asked for rather than on no job at all.
check: `test:rebuild` and `test:display` in `src/web/package.json` pass `--config playwright.{rebuild,display}.config.ts`, and the `slow-suites` job in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs both on `workflow_dispatch` and the nightly schedule — neither suite has been executed, so their green is unestablished

title: Fabric's derived per-character styles table is serialised into every saved text object
detail: FOUND WHILE CLOSING PLAN 1, by fixing a vacuous test rather than by driving the product. reference-theme.spec.ts's known-gap pin read only the TOP LEVEL of the saved scene, so after the starter became eight groups it reported no object carrying the table - on a document whose every text part carries one. Measured with a recursive read over a saved starter package: 30 objects carry a `styles` key. RE-MEASURED 2026-10-13 when the strip landed (Task 5.1): 28 objects, through the serialiser test helper rather than a recursive read of a saved package, and the starter has changed since the original measurement - so 30 is the 2026-10-08 reading, not a current count. Owner: scene-fabric/src/persist.ts, beside removeRuntimeText, which strips Fabric's own text cache but not this. The authored equivalent is vigiliaText.runs and nothing reads `styles` back, so it is unrevivable state in a shareable artifact - the same class as the blob: src leak below. The pin is now marked test.fail so it stays recorded and turns red the day it is fixed; it had never been marked, which is why it stayed green while asserting nothing. NOT FIXED here: fixing serialisation is scene-fabric's own surface and this session was closing plan 1. MARKER VERIFIED 2026-10-04: the prior report said test.fail 'did not take on this Playwright version'. It does - measured on 1.63.0 from test-results/summary.json: status 'failed', expectedStatus 'failed', stats.expected 2, unexpected 0. Both pins report as the pinned failures they are and go red the day the gap closes, so no change to the marking was needed.
check: `serialiseScene` in `scene-fabric/src/persist.ts` strips the derived per-character `styles` table from every saved text object, and `reference-theme.spec.ts`'s `test.fail` pin is gone — its case now asserts that no saved object carries a derived style table, and it passes in the browser run

title: A theme that fails validation is answered 404, vanishes from the library, and the editor reports success
detail: MEASURED AT THE BOUNDARY while fixing vg-095, and the most serious thing either of those agents found. A theme sitting on disk whose metadata carries a stale locale key, or a stray backgroundMedia.scale, is answered 404 Theme not found, does not appear in the library listing, and the editor's boot-theme.ts openQuietly then opens a DIFFERENT theme and reports success naming that one. The validation issues are discarded at host/src/themes/store.ts:452-460. So there are three distinct outcomes collapsed into one silent one: the theme does not exist, the theme exists and is invalid, and the theme loaded - all of them read to an author as 'Theme not found' or as a success message about the wrong theme. The editor is the worse half, because it is the only one that says something untrue rather than nothing. AGENTS.md asks a 404 to name the cause it can prove (ADR-0018), and this one cannot prove it because the issues were thrown away before the response was built - which is precisely the fix: keep them, and answer a refused theme with what refused it. An author who hand-edited a theme, or who has a theme from a build whose schema has since tightened, currently has no way to learn any of that.
check: `bootTheme` returns the library's validation issues and `editor-main` reports them, so a theme that fails validation is no longer answered as absent — the store's `ThemeValidationError` reaches the route as a `422` and the client's error carries its issues

title: The `locked` predicate has no owner: the lock manager owns writing the flag but not testing it, so eight modules spell the test themselves
detail:
FOUND by the reverse-direction read the user asked for after the manager-ownership survey ('does any manager turn out to be too small or narrow a concept to stand on its own and should be folded into another?'), run 2026-10-09 with docs/architecture/ownership.md as the yardstick. The answer to the question as put is no — every manager checked owns at least one decision nobody else owns — and these two rows are what the read actually found: the inverse defect, a shared fact that no module owns and every consumer re-spells. THE FACT. `object.get("locked")` is read in 11 non-test places across 8 modules: object-lock-manager/index.ts:40 (its private `isLocked`) and :81 (the one write); deletion-manager/index.ts:15 (`deletable`, `!== true`); clipboard-manager/index.ts:310 and :338 (`=== true`, twice inline); controls-manager/index.ts:82 and :157 (`!== true`, twice inline); indicator-manager/index.ts:93; editor-shell/bridge.ts:165; selection-inspector/index.ts:395; selection-inspector/per-kind-column.ts:634; selection-inspector/view.ts:466. By the map's own instrument — find the code that would reject a wrong value for a concept and ask whether it lives in the module the map names — this guard lives in eight modules and the map names none of them for it. object-lock-manager owns the flag's derivation from Fabric's transform flags (TRANSFORM_LOCKED/TRANSFORM_FREE, `hasControls` load-bearing) and the re-derivation on history load, but its predicate is private, so every other reader re-derives the vocabulary. WHY IT MATTERS. The polarity is not even consistent — `=== true` in five places, `!== true` in three — which is invisible today because both are falsy-safe, and stops being invisible the moment a third lock state exists (a partial lock, a group whose members differ). Then it is eight edit sites the map cannot list. This is the map's stated failure exactly: 're-spelling the set, or a subset of it, somewhere else is a second owner, and it fails quietly.' NOT ESTABLISHED: which module should own the predicate. object-lock-manager is the natural candidate but may sit above some of its readers in the import graph, in which case the fact belongs lower down (the same question vg-248 raises) — that ordering is the design decision the row waits on. NOT CLAIMED: that any current reader is wrong; all eleven agree on today's two states. OWNER: whoever owns the ownership map and the lock manager. COUNT AND STATUS CORRECTED BY THE CENSUS (2026-10-12): the predicate is spelled at 11 sites across 9 files (7 modules, and only 5 of those are manager directories), not 8, and all eleven agree on the two current states -- the risk is the THIRD state, not the present one. The census also records what this row still waits on: which module should own the predicate is unsettled because the import-graph ordering between object-lock-manager and its readers was never computed.

RULED 2026-10-12: RULED 2026-10-12 by the user: A LOWER SHARED MODULE OWNS THE PREDICATE, on the same reasoning as vg-248's ruling taken the same day -- the locked test is a Fabric fact rather than lock policy, so it goes where scene-fabric already carries shared facts, and no reader has to reach upward to object-lock-manager for it.

CORRECTED 2026-10-13 (Task 6.5a): the census's figures counted `object.get("locked")` alone - eleven occurrences, eight `=== true` and three `!== true`, one of the eight being the predicate's own body. Re-derived at HEAD, thirteen sites spell the test: the ten inline `get("locked")` reads (seven `=== true`, three `!== true`), plus `arrange.ts` (a truthiness test), `canvas-nudge.ts` (`!== true`) and `layer-tree.ts` (`=== true`), which reach the same flag through the instance property. All thirteen now call `isLocked` in `scene-fabric/src/object-lock.ts`, so `object.get("locked")` survives only inside that predicate.
check: `isLocked` in `scene-fabric/src/object-lock.ts` is the one `locked` predicate; the lock manager and every other reader call it, so no module spells the test itself.

title: The fact 'which collection holds this object' is spelled in four modules with three different return contracts, and its ActiveSelection companion in four more
detail:
FOUND by the reverse-direction read the user asked for after the manager-ownership survey ('does any manager turn out to be too small or narrow a concept to stand on its own and should be folded into another?'), run 2026-10-09 with docs/architecture/ownership.md as the yardstick. The answer to the question as put is no — every manager checked owns at least one decision nobody else owns — and these two rows are what the read actually found: the inverse defect, a shared fact that no module owns and every consumer re-spells. THE FACT. `parent instanceof Group` appears at four sites with three contracts: layer-manager/index.ts:24 `ownerOf` returning `Canvas | Group` (falling back to the canvas); deletion-manager/index.ts:25 returning `Canvas | Group | undefined` (its caller writes `ownerOf(object) ?? canvas`); editor-shell/layer-tree.ts:466 returning `Group | undefined`; and editor-shell/bridge.ts:278, which uses the same test to pick a child rather than a holder. Its companion — 'an ActiveSelection lives outside `_objects`, so move its members' — is spelled four times too: layer-manager/index.ts:30 (a named `targetsOf`), deletion-manager/index.ts:37 (inline), canvas-nudge.ts:46 (inline), history-manager/index.ts:114 (inline). deletion-manager's `ownerOf` is a near-copy of layer-manager's with a different signature, and its inline targets expression is layer-manager's named function retyped; the two modules do not import one another. WHY IT MATTERS. The comments on those functions record learned Fabric traps, not style: layer-manager/index.ts:18-22 ('a move issued on the canvas to a group child *inserts* it into the root and leaves it in both arrays — painted and serialised twice') and deletion-manager/index.ts:18-22 ('`Collection.remove` searches only its own `_objects` and returns an empty removal for anything else'). A trap documented in four places is a trap that gets fixed in one of them. The divergent signatures are the mechanism: a caller that forgets `?? canvas` silently gets `undefined` where the other three implementations would have handed it the canvas. NOTE. This is the same shape as vg-240 (one protocol implemented twice) at the helper scale, and it is why deletion-manager reads as a fold candidate — it is not too small, it shares a fact with layer-manager and neither owns it. NOT ESTABLISHED: which module should own it. The fact is pure Fabric knowledge rather than editor policy, so scene-fabric (which already carries shared Fabric facts, e.g. authored-box.ts) is a candidate alongside layer-manager. OWNER: whoever owns the map, with the layer and deletion managers.

RULED 2026-10-12: RULED 2026-10-12 by the user: SCENE-FABRIC OWNS THE FACT. Which collection holds an object is pure Fabric knowledge rather than editor policy, and scene-fabric already carries shared Fabric facts such as authored-box.ts, so the four return contracts collapse onto one helper there and a caller can no longer get undefined by forgetting to pass the canvas.

CORRECTED 2026-10-13 (Task 6.5a): the count was re-derived. The canvas-fallback holder contract was spelled in two modules, not four - `layer-manager`'s `ownerOf(canvas, object)` and `deletion-manager`'s `ownerOf(object)`, whose caller patched it with `?? canvas`; both now call `holderOf` in `scene-fabric/src/object-holder.ts`. The `ActiveSelection` companion is genuinely four: a named `targetsOf` in `layer-manager` and the inline expressions in `deletion-manager`, `canvas-nudge.ts` and `history-manager`, all now calling `targetsOf`. `layer-tree.ts`'s `ownerOf(root, id)` is not a third contract - it answers from the projection tree by id, with no canvas in scope - and `bridge.ts`'s `parent instanceof Group` picks a nested group's child rather than a holder.
check: `holderOf` and `targetsOf` in `scene-fabric/src/object-holder.ts` are the one spelling of which collection holds an object and of an `ActiveSelection`'s members; the layer, deletion, nudge and history callers use them.

title: object-actions.ts states the clipboard and deletion managers' lock refusal as its own eligibility rule, so eligibility is still a second owner of a decision made elsewhere
detail: FOUND BY the manager census (2026-10-12), carried as a `Discovered, not fixed:` trailer on commit a2fe5a89 and materialised here as its own row. object-actions.ts restates each manager's lock refusal at six eligibility sites, with a comment per site naming the manager it must agree with. That makes eligibility a second owner of every manager's refusal decision, kept in sync by hand and by comment, and no row named it. The census's rank 9 is the adjacent candidate; this row is the lock-refusal half of it. The correct behaviour is already specified by the one-owner-per-concept rule, so the fix is to ask the manager that refuses, or enumerate the refusal reasons once, and delete the restatements. CORRECTED 2026-10-12 by Task 9 candidate rank 9's review, which found this row wrong twice. It said eligibility re-states a manager's lock refusal at six sites 'with a comment per site naming the manager it must agree with': only four of the six re-state a refusal -- `:167` (`lock`) and `:174` (`unlock`) are affordances, and `object-lock-manager/index.ts:111`/`:116` guard only a null object and never read the lock state -- and those two sites carried no comment at all, checked against `800a244f`. Commit 6309f899 then collapsed the six inline expressions into two named predicates, one per condition, so the hand-synchronisation inside the file is gone. WHAT SURVIVES, and why the row stays open: `hasUnlockedSelection` still states ClipboardManager's and DeletionManager's refusal from outside both modules. The census offered two remedies and only the second was available -- asking the manager that refuses needs a design decision, because managers test a live `FabricObject` while `eligible` is a pure function of the Fabric-free `ObjectTarget` -- so that half defers to rank 1 and `vg-247`. SEVERITY unchanged: an agreement between modules that nothing enforces. READING 2026-10-13 (Task 6.2): `vg-247` landed, so the `locked` predicate has one owner — `scene-fabric/src/object-lock.ts` (`isLocked`) — and the bridge derives `ObjectTarget.locked` from it. `hasUnlockedSelection` reads that shared answer and states no manager's refusal, so what survives is the pure `ObjectTarget` question it actually owns. Nothing changed behaviour: the eleven lock readers and both managers agreed before and agree after, so no case could be red-first from a disagreement — the witness in `editor-shell.dom.test.ts` drives a real locked selection through both managers and turns red when the lock term moves on either side. OPEN QUESTION, deliberately not decided here: asking the managers themselves, the row's other remedy, still needs a design decision, because the managers test a live `FabricObject` while `eligible` is a pure function of the fabric-free `ObjectTarget`.
check: `hasUnlockedSelection` in `object-actions.ts` reads the shared `locked` predicate and states no manager's refusal; the witness in `editor-shell.dom.test.ts` drives both managers and turns red when the lock term moves on either side.

title: "Is this still referenced" is decided in two modules: dropDanglingBindings in editor-shell.ts and assetReferencedBy in asset-manager
detail: FOUND BY the manager census (2026-10-12), carried as a `Discovered, not fixed:` trailer on commit a2fe5a89 and materialised here as its own row. dropDanglingBindings lives in editor-shell.ts:126 and assetReferencedBy in asset-manager/index.ts:427, so one concept -- is this still referenced -- is decided in two modules with no row naming the split. This is the shape the census exists to find: a concept whose guard lives in a module the ownership map does not name for it. Whether the two agree today, and whether either is reachable without the other, was not established. READING 2026-10-13 (Task 6.2): established before the fix, because it decides the evidence. The two answer different questions about one scene — `dropDanglingBindings` asks which object ids the scene still holds, `assetReferencedBy` whether any object carries an asset reference — and neither calls nor imports the other, so each is reachable without the other. What was spelled twice is the walk both need: every object at any depth. The walk is now `sceneObjects` in `asset-manager/index.ts`, and `dropDanglingBindings` spends it instead of its own `visit`. They agree today in the sense the row asked about: both new cases pass against the unmodified source, so no case could be red-first from a disagreement, and the row closes on the case that fails if the fact is re-spelled. The cases pin the single answer at both call sites two groups down, and both go red when the walk is re-spelled root-only at either site. A third sibling the row does not name — `#holdsAsset` in `editor-session.ts` — belongs to another task's file.
check: `dropDanglingBindings` (`editor-shell.ts`) and `assetReferencedBy` (`asset-manager/index.ts`) both spend the one walk `sceneObjects` (`asset-manager/index.ts`), and the cases in `editor-shell.dom.test.ts` and `asset-manager/index.dom.test.ts` pin that answer two groups down, turning red when that walk is re-spelled shallow. The claim is scoped to the walk this question reads: other at-any-depth recursions exist for other questions and are not this row's (`vg-413`).

title: A globals edit reaches six owners on the palette path and three on the type path, so a renamed type preset leaves the inspector printing the old name
detail: FOUND by a read-only architecture survey the user asked for ('does any domain manager need clean-up — same domain spread across a few managers, a domain under another owner that should be its own'), run on 2026-10-09 with docs/architecture/ownership.md as the yardstick. VERIFIED BY ME from source, not taken from the survey. There is no owner for 'a globals edit must reach every consumer': editor-session.ts decides the receiver list inline, once per setter, and the lists disagree. #setPalette (editor-session.ts:1145-1158) calls shell.setGlobals, #runtime.setGlobals, charts.setGlobals, #newObjects.setGlobals, #artboard.setGlobals and #selection.setGlobals — SIX owners plus two renders. #setTypes (:1187-1194) calls three: shell, #runtime, #newObjects. #deleteType (:1219-1235) calls two — it omits #runtime as well. The consequence is behavioural: the inspector reads type-preset names and resolutions out of context.globals (per-kind-column.ts:545-546 and :607-608 call nameOfRef/resolveTypePreset on it), and selection-inspector/index.ts:524 is the only thing that updates that value. Because #setTypes never calls it, renaming a type preset leaves Spends printing the OLD name until an unrelated object:modified or selection event re-renders, which index.ts:491-517 lists as the only triggers. The source also asserts the wrong thing in prose: live-runtime.ts:103-108 says 'the session hands new globals to six owners (editor-session.ts:1041-1046)', true on one path of three, and the lines it cites now fall inside #release. NOT MEASURED: whether the missing charts.setGlobals and #artboard.setGlobals on the type path have their own visible staleness — I verified the inspector's only. SHAPE PRECEDENT: vg-058 (verified) is the same failure one instance smaller. OWNER: unassigned; the fix is one 'globals changed' fan-out the session owns, not four lists. SEVERITY: medium — a stale label that misreports what the document says.
check: editor-session.dom.test.ts 'reaches every globals consumer when a type preset is renamed' reads the inspector's Spends line after a rename

title: The save's picture fallback is written twice: #save spells the expression inline while #writeLibrary calls #picture
detail: FOUND by a read-only architecture survey the user asked for ('does any domain manager need clean-up — same domain spread across a few managers, a domain under another owner that should be its own'), run on 2026-10-09 with docs/architecture/ownership.md as the yardstick. The smallest finding it returned and the clearest instance of a rule written twice. editor-session.ts:734-738 defines #picture, and :723 — inside #save — spells the same expression inline, (await this.#capture(options)) ?? this.#thumbnail, instead of calling it; only #writeLibrary (:802) calls #picture. title: Three owners of 'list the document's tokens by name' is the shape that let vg-093 exist
detail:
FOUND WHILE FIXING vg-093 and vg-102, which is the third round of the same defect in this repo. artboard-panel.ts:519, palette-manager/panel.ts:214 and chart-manager/panel.ts:324 each build their own option list over the same globals, and each is a place a label can come out as an id instead of a name. vg-088 fixed runs.ts, vg-093 fixed the colour dropdown beside it, vg-102 fixed four resolution lines, and the next surface to print a raw ref will be one of these three. That is the point: the defect has been fixed three times in individual surfaces and the shape that permits it is untouched. ONE OWNER of 'list the document's references by name' is the fix, and it is a design call rather than a patch — the three lists differ in what they filter and what they do on an unresolvable token, so consolidating them means deciding what the shared function owes each caller. Worth noting what the fix already established: a token the author has DELETED is the one case where the raw ref is correct, because it is the only identifier left, and that case is pinned by a test.

RULED 2026-10-12: RULED 2026-10-12 by the user: ONE FUNCTION IN THE TOKEN OWNER, AND EACH CALLER PASSES ITS OWN FILTER. The function resolves a label from the document's tokens and returns the raw ref only for a token the author deleted -- the one case the existing fix established and a test pins -- so the three lists stop being three places a label can print as an id. What each surface filters stays at that surface, because that is what actually differs between them.
check: `paletteTokenOptions` in `renderer-core/src/theme/palette-tokens.ts` is the one function that lists the document's tokens by name; the artboard, the chart paint rows, the inspector's material fields and the run editor all call it, each passing its own filter.

title: The map gives the artboard-to-viewport transform to renderer-core, but no editor module calls it — the camera re-implements contain and centring itself
detail:
FOUND by a read-only architecture survey the user asked for ('does any domain manager need clean-up — same domain spread across a few managers, a domain under another owner that should be its own'), run on 2026-10-09 with docs/architecture/ownership.md as the yardstick. VERIFIED BY ME with a repo-wide grep, and it is the cleanest instance of an owner that serves someone else. ownership.md:76 gives 'The artboard-to-viewport transform — contain/cover scale, letterbox bars, cover crop' to renderer-core/src/artboard.ts, whose computeArtboardTransform (:46) is guarded (it throws RangeError on a degenerate viewport, artboard.test.ts:269). Nothing in the editor calls it: the only callers are renderer-core/src/scene/mount.ts:83 and scene-fabric/src/scene.ts:116, i.e. the plan and player path. Meanwhile the editor's camera re-implements the rule, unguarded: viewport-manager/index.ts fitScaleFor (:209-214) re-derives contain as Math.min(box.width / board.width, box.height / board.height) clamped to MIN_ZOOM/MAX_ZOOM (:11-12), and fitTransformIn (:224-237) re-derives the centring. The prose agrees with the code and disagrees with the map: editor-shell.ts:591 says 'the authored fit mode belongs to the player's letterbox'. So the map's Editor table has a row whose owner the editor never uses, and the editor's version of that invariant has no single owner and none of the guard's refusals. NOT ESTABLISHED: whether the editor's fit is deliberately a different rule (fit to the display's screen rather than the host — the comment at :230-233 says exactly that) or a copy that drifted; if it is deliberate it needs its own row and its own guard, and if it is a copy the two should meet. OWNER: whoever owns the map, plus viewport-manager. SEVERITY: medium — the contain rule is an invariant and only one of its two copies is guarded.

RULED 2026-10-12: RULED 2026-10-12 by the user: DELIBERATE -- the editor's fit is a different rule from the renderer-core transform, and it gets its own row and its own guard. The editor fits to the display's screen rather than to the host, which is what the camera's centring comment states, so the map's Editor row stops claiming renderer-core owns the editor's case, and the editor's contain rule gains the refusals the renderer-core version already has -- today only one of the two copies is guarded.
check: the editor's own fit in `viewport-manager/index.ts` refuses a board with no frameable area, exactly as `computeArtboardTransform` does, and the map's editor row no longer claims renderer-core owns the editor's case.

title: `importImage`'s `scale` option is inert: the caller passes `image-contain` and the body never reads it, so an imported image's fit is not what the caller asked for
detail:
FOUND BY Task 4's independent review of the dead-code sweep (2026-10-12), verifying a claim the sweep's implementer raised and deliberately did not file, at HEAD `93bb2c5f`. THE SITES, each read at HEAD: `packages/editor/src/image-manager/index.ts:13` declares `readonly scale?: "image-contain" | "image-cover" | "scale-montage"`, and it is the ONLY occurrence of the word `scale` in that file, so the body reads `options.source`, `options.withoutAdding` and `options.withoutSave` and never `options.scale`; `packages/editor/src/asset-manager/index.ts:91` calls it with `scale: "image-contain"`. CONSEQUENCE: an imported image is fitted by whatever the body does unconditionally, while the call site reads as though it chose the fit. INERTNESS IS ESTABLISHED; THE INTENDED BEHAVIOUR IS NOT, which is why this is a row rather than a fix on the fly: nothing read says whether `scale` was meant to drive the placed object's scaling or the decoded `FabricImage`'s sizing, or whether the union is left over from a design that moved elsewhere. It also owns two `unreachable-branch` rows the sweep's candidate report carries, which cannot be resolved until the option either gains a reader or is removed. NOT ESTABLISHED: whether any test asserts the option is accepted-and-ignored, and whether a `scale: "image-cover"` call site was ever intended. VERIFIED by the review report at `.superpowers/sdd/2026-10-12-the-dead-code-sweep/task-4-review.md`, which located the same three sites independently.

RULED 2026-10-12: RULED 2026-10-12 by the user: REMOVE IT. The scale option is inert -- no reader, and no call site can tell what it chose -- so it is removed rather than given a reader, which also resolves the two unreachable-branch candidate rows it owns.
check: `importImage` declares no `scale` option: the caller no longer passes `image-contain`, and no file names a fit the body never reads.

title: `--cite`'s placement check admits a marker that drifts to any `###` subsection of its mapped `##`, because the rule is a prefix test and the spec's mapping names only `## Components` for `§6`
detail: FOUND BY the scoped re-review of the design-md final fix round (2026-10-11), residual R2, ruled acceptable-not-fixed. WHAT: scripts/design-md.mjs's placement rule is `expected.every((heading, i) => path[i] === heading)`, a prefix test, so a marker mapped at a bare `##` stays legal anywhere under that `##` -- moving `§7` off the top of `## Layout` down to `### The rail` (same section) still passes `--cite`, which the re-review reproduced as exit 0. WHY NOT TIGHTENED: DESIGN.md holds a *legitimate* arrangement of exactly that shape -- `§6`, the icon vocabulary, is mapped to `## Components` and sits under `## Components -> ### Icons` (DESIGN.md heading `### Icons` at 491, its `<!-- §6 -->` marker at 493), as do `§7.1`-`§7.8` under their `## Layout` subsections. Requiring a marker's path to equal the mapped path exactly would reject that correct document, so the prefix test is the strictest check that does not false-positive on the current file. WHY IT IS LOW: the drift stays inside the mapped section, `§3` (the one `###`-mapped number) is checked exactly, and every launch-fail direction still fails closed. WHAT WOULD CLOSE IT: the spec's section-mapping table recording the exact `###` a marker sits under (e.g. `§6 -> ### Icons`), with the rule tightened to path equality.
check: `design-md.mjs`'s `--cite` placement check no longer admits a marker that drifts to any `###` subsection of its mapped `##`: the rule is now path equality, and the spec's section mapping names the exact `###` each marker sits under.
